I NTRODUCTION W ith a view to addressing and, wherever possible, avoiding interpersonal conflicts simple and reliable informal mechanism s consisting in Facilitation and Mediation are required through the provision of external Mediators . P revention I n order to create a positive working environment, the Agency’s focus in the first instance is on conflict prevention. If and when tensions arise, they need to be addressed as early as possible in order to avoid long- lasting conflicts and aggravation. In t he case of interpersonal difficulties, it is essential that conflicts are addressed as early as possible and at the lowest level of intervention. Ideally, raising the matter directly with the person concerned is the best way to resolve issues . I nformal and formal mechanisms As t here is no one way of pre venting or resolving conflict, d ifferent informal and formal mechanisms exist to address conflicts when they arise and need to be applied according to the specific circumstances of each case. I t is theref ore strongly advised to seek the resolution of the problem through informal mechanisms first with the possible involvement of the Conflict Navigato

e specific circumstances of each case. I t is theref ore strongly advised to seek the resolution of the problem through informal mechanisms first with the possible involvement of the Conflict Navigators and/or the Mediators. T he advantage of the informal procedure over the formal procedure lies in the poss ibly of finding an amicable settlement of the situation in shorter timeframes thereby avoiding any further deterioration in the working environment. H aving recourse to the Mediators does not preclude application of the formal procedures provided for in the Staff Regulations, Rules and Instructions. 2. P OLICY I t is the Agency’s policy to introduce informal mechanism s (Facilitation and Mediation) allowing the resolution of interpersonal disputes within the Agency. 3. S COPE T he present Instruction applies to all cases of interpersonal dispute in the workplace between : − st aff members ; and − staff members and on - site contractors ’ personnel, or research fellows or trainees i rrespective of if the reference to articles in the Staff Regulations applies only to ESA staff. DEFINITIONS Within the scope of this Instruction, the following definit ions apply: Applicant to Facilitation or Mediation is a person within the scope of the instruction defined in section 3 above that is applying to the Coordinating Mediator to resolve an interpersonal conflict b etween himself and another P arty. Parties to Facilitation or Mediation are persons within the scope of the instruction defined in section 3 above that have recourse to one of these informal mechanisms to resolve an interpersonal conflict between them. Facilitation is the use of a neutral third party to help P arties identify potential issues ( such as tensions between viewpoints, interpersonal or other relationship issues) and facilitate constructive communication, collaborative problem solving and decision - making. Mediation is the use of a neutral third party to help P arties reach a voluntary resolution of a dispute which P arties have been unwilling or unable to resolve on their own. Mediation is a structured process that starts with the signing of a mediation agreement, after which the me diator will engage the P arties in confidential discussions based on interests rather than positions and help them negotiate an amicable settlement. A successful mediation results in a written, signed agreement set

gage the P arties in confidential discussions based on interests rather than positions and help them negotiate an amicable settlement. A successful mediation results in a written, signed agreement settling all matters in dispute. Mediators re fer s to both the Coordinating and Local Mediators , whose Terms of Reference and Status are defined in Annex 1 . Conflict Navigators are staff members with roles and responsibilities with regard to conflict prevention and resolution appointed by the Department in charge of personnel matters following consultation with the Staff A ssociation. 5. PRINCIPLES 5. 1 Voluntary participation Participation to Facilitation and Mediation is done on a voluntary basis. 5.2 Mediator’s right to decline a case Mediators may decline to examine any case submitted to them, stating their reasons for doing so . 5. 3 On - going d isciplinary p roceedings Where the Administration has initiate d disciplinary proceedings in accordance with Staff Regulation 26, the Mediators shall not be authorised to examine a case submitted to them if the case concerns the alleged offence subject to disciplinary proceedings. 5. 4 Impartiality The Coordinating Mediator and the Local Mediators shall perform their duties in a fu lly independent manner. The Mediators are neutral and impartial, which implies they do not take position or judge who is wrong or right. While in office, t

Mediators shall perform their duties in a fu lly independent manner. The Mediators are neutral and impartial, which implies they do not take position or judge who is wrong or right. While in office, they shall not hold any post or carry out any activity that might be considered to affect their impartiality. Such obligation shall continue indefinitely after the termination of their appointment. 5. 6 Security Marking of Communications C ommunications between the Mediators and between a Mediator and an A pplicant or any other person involved in a case treated by the Mediators are considered ESA Unclassified – Personnel in Confidence and shall therefore only be disclosed in accordance with section 3.4.6 of the ESA Security Directives and if duly authorised by the Media tors. 5. 7 Unauthorised disclosure U nauthorised disclosure by a staff member may constitute an offence liable to disciplinary action. U nauthorised disclosure by on - site contractor personnel may result in them being barred from ESA sites and in the termination of the contract with the Contractor responsible for such personnel. 6 . R OLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES 6.1 Coordinating Mediator T he Coordinating Mediator is in charge of the coordination of a network of Local Mediators appointed by the Director General and established in the countries where ESA has its Establishments. T he Coordinating Mediator shall examine the applications and endeavour to bring about an amicable settlement between the P arties within reasonable time limits using the two alternative dispute resolution techniques: Facilitation or Mediation. S hould the Coordinating Mediator find that it is not possible to propose Facilitation or Mediation, he/she shall inform the Parties accordingly. 6.2 Local Mediators T he Local Mediat or s shall examine the applications and endeavour to bring about an amicable settlement between the P arties within reasonable time limits using the two alternative dispute resolution techn iques : Facilitation or M ediation . S hould the Local Mediator find that it is not possible to propose F acilitation or Mediation, he/she shall inform the P arties accordingly. 6.3 Conflicts Navigators C onflict Navigators shall provide the Coordinating Mediator and the Local Mediators with practical arrangement s and administrative support they require in order to carry out their duties. U pon first contact, the Mediator shall begin any attempt of interpersonal dispute resolution b y lis tening to the Applicant in an open mind and understanding manner . As a first step, wher e a ppropriate, the Mediator shall try, by identifying and reframing issues and by developing a range of options, to help the A pplicant develop new ways to solve the problems on his/her own accord . Should such an approach prove unsuccessful , the Mediator shall attempt to reach a n am icable settlement through F acilitation or Mediation as described below. 2. T he A pplicant may however, in the course of the F acilitation or M ediation proce ss, decide to safeguard his/her right to appeal by submitting a claim to the Director General within the time limits and subject to the procedure set out in the Staff Regulations, Rules and Instructions. The appeal shall contain a request for a suspension of the claim procedure pending the finalization of the F acilitation or M ediation process . 3. ESA Director General’s Office _______ E SA/ADMIN/IPOL -WO RK( 202 3 ) 1 Att.: Annex Paris, 1 st February 202 3 ( Original: E nglish) Distribution: a ll staff E SA u nclassified – “ Releasable to the P ublic” Policy on Reporting Unwanted Conduct and Investigating Harassment at ESA 1. INT RODUCTION The A gency’s most valuable resource is its staff. The Agency strives for a work environment that is free of harassment , and where all persons are treated with respect and dignity. This means having a healthy and safe organisation based on values such as integrity, honour and trust. Dive rsity is a richness and brings added value for the Agency. H owever, ensuring a harmonious working environment with a diverse population requires a thoughtful attitude, since the notion of what is acceptable behaviour may vary from one culture to the next. This requires an organisational culture where everyone feels a personal responsibility to uphold the dignity of all colleagues. Wi th a view to addressing and, wherever possible, avoiding interpersonal conflicts, it is strongly encouraged to seek resolution of those issues informally. For this purpose, staff members are free to get support from the stakeholders whose roles and responsibilities are defined under Section 6 below. In addition, the Agency has established a Policy on Facilitation and Mediation, whereby simple and reliable informal mechan

eholders whose roles and responsibilities are defined under Section 6 below. In addition, the Agency has established a Policy on Facilitation and Mediation, whereby simple and reliable informal mechanisms for dispute resolution are provided for (cf. ESA/ADMIN/IPOL - WORK(2019)1). Having recourse to the informal resolution of interpersonal issues does not preclude application of the formal procedure provided for in the present Instruction. 2. POL ICY It is the Agency’s Policy to protect the dignity of every person working at ESA against any form of unwanted conduct and harassment as well as to implement preventive measures conducive of a respectful workplace . This Policy is also to introduce a fair and transparent procedure to deal with the reporting of unwanted conduct and occurrences of harassment. ESA/ADMIN/IPOL -WO RK ( 202 3 ) 1 Pag e 2 3. SCOPE OF A PPLICATION In light of the definitions detailed in Section 4 below, the present Instruction applies to s ituations of harassment involving one or several staff members as party, i.e. , either as the person(s) subject to the occurrences reported, or as the person(s) concerned by t he report. In addition, the occurrences reported must relate to the staff members’ functions or having taken place at ESA’s premises. Under this understanding, the present Instruction applies to cases between: - staff members, or - staff members and n

st relate to the staff members’ functions or having taken place at ESA’s premises. Under this understanding, the present Instruction applies to cases between: - staff members, or - staff members and non - staff members . even if the reference to articles in the Staff Regulations, Rules and Instructions applies only to ESA staff members. 4. DEF INITIONS Wi thin the scope of this Instruction, the following definitions apply. 4.1 Harassment Har assment is defined as any improper behaviour that is reasonably expected or perceived as offending, intimidating, hostile, or undermining the dignity or adversely affecting the physical or mental health of a person or a group of persons . Harassment often implies a series of incidents. It may come from colleagues on an equal footing, as well as superiors and subordinates. H arassment may take the form of verbal or written abuse of a degrading or offensive nature or of intimidation or threats, may occur for a variety of reasons and may be directed at an individual or at a group of persons. Harassment may take various forms, such as those described in the sections hereinafter . Harassment might have various consequences for the person who is subject to it or who feels they are being subjected to it: - they become isolated and social relationships tend to deteriorate - they make more mistakes, can no longer concentrate, become less productive,

ect to it or who feels they are being subjected to it: - they become isolated and social relationships tend to deteriorate - they make more mistakes, can no longer concentrate, become less productive, are demotivated, etc.; - their professional development is hindered, career jeopardised, their very job put on the line; - they suffer mental and physical health problems. The a dverse consequences do not just affect the Person(s) Subject to Harassment, but also impact on other colleagues and on the institution itself: loss of expertise, staff transfers, fall in productivity, absenteeism, harming the image of the institution, etc. For these reasons, whichever the form it may take, harassment is unacceptable, and occurrences of harassment should be reported . ESA/ADMIN/IPOL -WO RK( 202 3 ) 1 Pag e 3 Cer tain kinds of behaviour may hurt certain people without constituting harassment. For example, a remark, a dispute, a clash of personalities, professional stress caused by overwork or poor organisation, a management decision (such as redeployment or a transfer), which is difficult to accept, a duly substantiated negative assessment, even repeated, are not prima facie considered harassment. For the purpose of the present Instruction and the Annex, it is understood that , even where the present Instruction refers to “ h arassment” , the occurre nces reported to the Head of Human Resources Department remain allegations 1 until establishment of the facts by the Investigator(s) and until the Investigator(s) conclude that the allegations are substantiated at the end of the investigation procedure. a) S ex ual Harassment Sex ual harassment is defined as any form of verbal or physical conduct or gesture of a sexual nature, or any other conduct of a sexual nature that is reasonably expected to be, or reasonably perceived as being, offending, humiliating, intimidating, hostile, or as undermining the dignity of individuals at work. - Physical conduct of a sexual nature is regarded as meaning unwanted physical contact ranging from e.g., unnecessary touching, patting or pinching or brushing against another employee’s body; it also includes coercion into having sexual intercourse. - Verbal conduct of a sexual nature may include unwelcome sexual advances, propositions, or pressure to engage in sexual activity, offensive f lirtation, suggestive remark

o having sexual intercourse. - Verbal conduct of a sexual nature may include unwelcome sexual advances, propositions, or pressure to engage in sexual activity, offensive f lirtation, suggestive remarks, innuendoes, or lewd comments. - Non - verbal conduct of a sexual nature refers to inter alia the display of pornographic or sexually suggestive pictures, objects or written materials, leering, or making sexually suggestive gestu res. - Sexual harassment may also correspond to conduct that denigrates, ridicules, intimidates, or is physically abusive of persons because of their gender, such as derogatory or degrading abuse, insults which are gender - related, or offensive comments about appearance , body parts or clothing . b) Mor al Harassment Mor al harassment is defined as any type of conduct that is reasonably expected or perceived as abusive and repeated over a sustained period on the part of an individual or group of individuals, which , through behaviour, words ( whether spoken or written ) , 1 Except when the facts are clearly established, cf. This ki nd of h arassment m ay per tain e.g. , t o ethnicity, c olour, r eligion, ge nder, s exual orientation, or disability in accordance with Section 4. 2 below . c) Bullying Bullying is a form of harassment where an individual abuses a position of influence over another person. It involves persistent criticism and personal abuse, both in public or in private, which humiliates and demeans the individual gradually eroding their s ense of self. It can take many different forms. T he following are so m e other exa mples o f be haviour, w hic h may r easonably be perceived as bul lying: - Shou ting at an individual - Picking on one person when there is a common problem - Consistently undermining someone and their ability to do their job. d) Mobbi ng Mobbi ng means ganging up on someone or psychologically undermining them at work. It can be less overt than bullying and it may not even be obvious that a person is being victimised in this way. It is characterised by somewhat subtler behaviour than bullyin g by, for example, socially isolating the person(s) or pushing them into a helpless or defenceless position. It involves an individual or a “mob” of people who deliberately set out to make the working life of a colleague miserable. The following are some other examples of behaviour which may reasonably be perceived by a person as constituting mobbing: - colleagues do not talk to them, they are isolated or ignored (e.g. a person has limited possibilities to maintain social contact); - others gossip about them, ridicule them or make fun of them such that a person may have difficulty maintaining their personal reputation, or - they are not given any work or are given meaningless tasks (there are adverse effects on their occupational situation). 4.2 Discrimination Discrimination is any unfair treatment or arbitrary distinction based on a person’s race, sex, ethnic origin, nationality, political, philosophical or religious opinions , health, disability, gender or sexual orientation, age, or other status. It may be an isolated event affecting one person or a group of persons or may manifest itself through harassment as defined above. PRI NCIPLES 5.1 Prevention Harassment is not tolerated at ESA and the Agency is committed to prevent inappropriate behaviour in the workplace . For this purpose, and in addition to prohibiting harassment and providing adequate measures to address it, t he Agency’s focus is also on conflict prevention. In order to create a harmonious working environment and mitigate the risks of interpersonal issues , individuals are encouraged to get acquainted with the ESA Charter of Values and the ESA Behaviour Guide . They are also encouraged to follow training to develop their behavioural skills, notably in the field of interpersonal communication and conflict management . ESA/ADMIN/IPOL -WO RK ( 202 3 ) 1 Pag e 6 In the case where an individual is facing interpersonal iss ues , and where appropriate , it is strongly advised as a first step to seek the resolution of the problem through informal procedures. This policy is based on all ESA Member States participating – having due regard to their financial contribution - in an equitable manner to the successful creation of a strong and competitive European industrial base for space activities. In order to provide for an equal and transparent treatment of all companies and furthermore to ensure an effective and accurate reporting on the industrial return statistics to the Member States, the objective of ESA audits in relation to the nationality o f companies, is to be assured or alternatively obtain evidence that an enterprise can effectively be considered to belong to specific ESA Member States, allowing as such the (parts of the - ) contracts awarded to this company to be coun

The descriptions of direct and indirect cost below only serve to identify those costs, but do not prescribe a definitive structure to be followed. The determination of the hours or other suitable recovery base(s) for the direct and indirect costs used in ascertaining the rates, will be representative of a business operating in a competitive and steady environment, corresponding to the size and structure of other companies in the same country operating in that sector. The hours assumed for the rates and overheads calculation shall be based on reasonable and coherent values, in comparison with the historical performance of the company, of the following parameters: • A reasonable level of personnel ‘Availability’, i.e. ratio of actual worked hours and theoretical work hours per year, in consideration of averages in the same Country as the audited contractor, and specific employment agreements. • A reasonable level of ‘Utilization’, i.e. ratio of sellable hours and worked hours of Direct Labour Categories or Cost Centres, in consideration of a normal business level. • A reasonable level of ‘Productivity’, i.e. ratio of sellable hours and worked hours of all personnel, including external workforce and allocated group centralised functions, in consideration of a normal business level. 3.0.1 Reasonability The rates and overheads allocated to each unit of production shall not be signi

A rticle XVII of the Convention establishes an arbitration proce dure for settling disputes that may arise between two or more ESA Member States or between any of them and the Agency, concerning the interpretation or application of the Convention, including its Annexes, and the disputes referred to in Article XXVI of Annex 1 to the Convention . This arbitration proce dure may be used if it has not been possible to settle the dispute amicably through the Council. T hese additional arbitration rules were unanimously adopt ed by the ESA Council during its 66 th meeting held on 12 and 13 De cember 1984. ESA UNCLASSIFIED – Releasable to public REGULATIONS OF THE EUROPEAN SPACE AGENCY RULES ON INFORMATION, DATA AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY According to the provisions of the ESA Convention, it is part of the Agency 's remit to facilitate the exchange of the scientific and technical information pertaining to space research and technology, considering that such substantial scientific and technical information contributes to the objective s of the Agency towards improvin g the competitiveness of European industry while ensuring that scientific results are made available . The Rules on Information, Data and Intellectual Property, as adopted by Council on 19 December 2001 under the reference ESA/C/CLV/Rules 5 (Final), are de signed to promote access to information and data and to cover the use of Intellectual Property resulting from Agency's activities, while fully taking into account the provisions of the Convention and the interests of the Member States and of persons and b odies under their jurisdiction. These Rules on Information, Data and Intellectual Property are, as appropriate, complemented by other Regulations and Rules such as the G eneral C lauses and C onditions for ESA contracts, the ESA Staff Regulations, Rules and Instructions, the ESA Security Regulations and Directives. The Rules on Information, Data and Intellectual Property are herewith attached. ESA/REG/00 8 Paris, 23

ESA/REG/00 8 Paris, 23 April 2014 eCPB-2014-0596 ESA/ REG/008 Rules on Information, Data and Intellectual Property General Principles These Rules are designed to promote access to Information and Data and use of Intellectual Property resulting from Agency activities, while fully taking into account the provisions of the Convention and the interests of the Member States and of Persons and Bodies under their Jurisdiction. The protection of Information and Data by Intellectual Property an d its licensing are internationally recognised as the most appropriate and effective means of ensuring that its value is preserved and that it is effectively exploited. The Agency considers that the originators of Information, Data and Intellectual Proper ty are best placed to exploit it. It is therefore provided that Information, Data and Intellectual Property developed by Agency staff in the course of their duties is owned by the Agency and that Information, Data and Intellectual Property originated by a Contractor to the Agency is owned by the Contractor. These Rules define circumstances in which there are to be rights of access, use and disclosure of Information, Data and Intellectual Property free of charge (without

gency is owned by the Contractor. These Rules define circumstances in which there are to be rights of access, use and disclosure of Information, Data and Intellectual Property free of charge (without prejudice to reimbursement of any co sts necessarily incurred by a contractor) or in exchange for a reduced charge, reflecting the financial contributions made by the Agency and its Member States towards its creation. As a specific exception to the above - mentioned general rule, in certain ca ses, given the special nature of the Agency’s activities, the Council may decide that the ownership of Information, Data and Intellectual Property may remain with the Agency. In these cases access and use shall be available free of charge to Member States and Persons and Bodies under their Jurisdiction, without limitation to space applications. It is thus maintained by the Agency as a pool of knowledge and experience, as an appropriate and effective means by which the Agency can support the worldwide compet itiveness of the European industry. Where the interests of the Agency are best served by making specific Information, Data and Intellectual Property available freely to the worldwide community, Council may decide to adopt the appropriate policy accordingl y. The distinction drawn by the Convention between the property of the Agency and other Information, Data and Intellectual Property is considered to be of central importance and is understood as specifically providing for acc ess, disclosure and use which are not free of charge, wherever it is appropriate for charges to be implemented. RULES AND REGULATIONS (a) The Director General shall ensure and define rules and regulations for the respect of any Intellectual Property right owned by the Agency or by any other natural or legal person in compliance with national and international rules of law in order to prevent any unauthorised use, which includes, but is not limited to, manufactu ring, selling, publication, modification, transmission, reproduction, distribution, performance, display or exploitation in whole or in part. (b) The Director General shall define rules and regulations laying down the basic principles and minimum security standards for safeguarding Information and Data held by the Agency from loss of confidentiality, availability or integrity. (d) To ensure access by the Agency, for its own requirements in the field of space research and technology and their applications or for the purpose of the Agency’s own security, to classified information, the unauthorised disclosure of which could damage the security interests of the Agency or those of one or more Member States, t he Agency shall conclude a security agreement with its Member States and the Director General shall, with the assistance of national Experts, develop specific provisions for the standard protection of such information.
